reasons.17: Gives full SPE preconcentration procedure for chromium‑plating wastewater (matrix-specific: high-strength industrial), including cartridge type, conditioning, sample volume, wash, elution, and flow rate prior to UPLC‑MS/MS.
reasons.4: Describes SPE cleanup/preconcentration of PFAS from ion-exchange regeneration wastewater with high inorganic salt; includes cartridge type, conditioning, sample volume, wash, elution, and flow control, illustrating matrix-driven protocol choices.

reasons.11: Discusses membrane separation and evaporative separation (membrane distillation) as concentrating PFAS due to low vapor pressure; directly relevant to routes that concentrate rather than destroy PFAS.
reasons.12: Explains electrodialysis as an electrical membrane process that concentrates PFAS and notes that electrical treatment can degrade PFAS whereas filtration only concentrates; distinguishes separation vs degradation within membrane/electrical methods.
reasons.16: Classifies separation-based vs destruction-based technologies and lists ion exchange, GAC, nanofiltration, and reverse osmosis as separation methods that do not destroy PFAS; includes membrane distillation as a physical separation route.
reasons.20: Explicitly categorizes PFAS removal into separation-based and destruction-based technologies and notes that nanofiltration and reverse osmosis are separation processes that do not eliminate PFAS, generating secondary waste streams.
reasons.28: Identifies nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, and adsorption-based membranes as the typical membrane technologies for PFAS removal and emphasizes their integration with other approaches, implying they are primarily separation/concentration steps rather than destructive.

reasons.8: Directly states equilibrium/contact times needed for long- vs short-chain PFAS with PAC (60–120 min for long-chain to 80–90% equilibrium; 240 min for short-chain to 85%), highly relevant to planning contact time when treating both.
reasons.2: Provides detailed PAC kinetic behavior at 10 mg/L: ~70% removal within 30 min, ~constant by 240 min, and notes some PFAS require 360 min to reach 90% adsorption, informing minimum contact times.
reasons.1: Gives PAC dose–response at fixed 30 min contact time, including that long-chain PFAS can meet regulatory targets at 30 mg/L and 30 min, while short-chain require higher doses and have slower adsorption (PFPeA), relevant to balancing dose vs contact time.
reasons.7: Describes PAC dosage tests at 30 min contact time for multiple PFAS, showing poor short-chain removal at low dose and better performance at higher dose, useful context for how much extra contact/dose short chains may need.
reasons.12: Notes that PFAS removals with PAC increase with both PAC dose and contact time and distinguishes behavior of long- vs short-chain PFAS, supporting the need for longer contact when targeting both.
reasons.21: Discusses how short contact time (15 min) favored short-chain PFAS diffusion vs long-chain in GAC/AER, illustrating that required contact time can differ by chain length and that too-short times disadvantage long-chain removal.
reasons.28: Reports that both 1 h and 24 h contact times were effective for long-chain PFAS (~100% removal) and that equilibrium may be reached relatively quickly (<1 h) for some PFAS, giving additional kinetic benchmarks.
reasons.30: States that even with extended contact times, PAC/GAC often remove only 15–40% of short-chain PFAS, underscoring that simply increasing contact time may not be sufficient and that design must account for limited short-chain sorption.
reasons.27: Notes PAC has somewhat higher adsorption efficiency for short-chain PFAS than GAC due to shorter internal diffusion paths, supporting the choice of PAC and the importance of kinetics/contact time for short chains.
reasons.3: Summarizes literature that AC removal of short-chain PFAS is often low and variable, with specific equilibrium removal ranges, reinforcing limitations of PAC for short-chain PFAS even at equilibrium contact times.

reasons.10: Direct fixed-bed GAC study explicitly stating that higher EBCT steepened PFAS breakthrough curves but did not change apparent adsorption capacity, answering whether longer EBCT necessarily improves performance.
reasons.4: Full-scale GAC data showing no consistent differences in PFAS adsorption capacity between EBCTs of 13 and 26 min, strong evidence that longer EBCT does not always yield better performance.
reasons.8: Full-scale GAC plant study linking flow rate/EBCT to PFAS removal, noting diminishing benefits at higher EBCT for a young filter, useful for understanding when longer EBCT stops improving performance.
reasons.24: Conclusions from same Park et al. study as ID 10 reiterating that longer EBCTs caused steeper breakthroughs with similar BV50 and even enhanced chromatographic desorption for some PFAS, reinforcing that more EBCT is not always better.
reasons.2: Results section discussing pilot GAC studies with specific EBCTs (6.1 and 10 min) and their role in realistic PFAS breakthrough, useful contextual evidence on EBCT ranges and performance assessment.
reasons.21: Pilot-scale GAC system description with EBCT fixed at 10 min; useful as realistic operational context for typical EBCT used in PFAS GAC treatment, to compare against other EBCTs.
reasons.1: Methods/background noting typical EBCT ranges for PFAS remediation (10–20 min) vs drinking water filter-adsorbers (5–10 min), helpful for framing expectations about EBCT and performance but not giving direct performance comparison.
reasons.3: Introductory description that EBCT is a traditional design parameter (5–15 min) for GAC systems; useful for context on how EBCT is used but not directly on whether longer EBCT improves PFAS removal.
reasons.18: Life-cycle analysis noting that adsorbent performance on a bed-volume basis did not vary significantly across sites with different conditions, indirectly supporting that factors other than EBCT dominate performance.
reasons.26: Review text discussing contact time and DOM effects on PFAS adsorption, including mention of pre-equilibrium (15 min) vs longer contact, providing ancillary insight into when increased contact time matters.
